newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: SLOVAK FINMIN SAYS MULLING FOREIGN BOND ISSUES.
newsitem.headline: SLOVAK FINMIN SAYS MULLING FOREIGN BOND ISSUES.

text.p: The Slovak Finance Ministry said it will have to issue state securities denominated in Slovak crowns on foreign markets this year to help cover the growing state budget deficit, daily Pravda reported on Friday.

"It will be necessary to issue crown-denominated state securities on foreign markets, otherwise there is a danger that debt servicing will take more than one-third of budget revenues next year," Pravda quoted Deputy Finance Minister Peter Stanek as saying.
Stanek said the current state budget deficit was close to an "unbearable stage", adding that sources outside the domestic arena will be needed to refinance the shortfall.

"We have to say that it will be impossible to refinance the deficit from the existing sources. The Slovak banking sector does not have 25 billion crowns which we will need (for deficit covering) by the end of this year," Stanek said.

At present, the finance ministry uses treasury bills and one-year state bonds as the main tools to cover the budget deficit, which widened to 17.936 billion crowns for the January-July period of 1997, from 13.209 billion in the first six months last year.
The ministry has been accepting high yields in state securities auctions over the past few months, resulting from the liquidity shortage on the Slovak interbank market.

The finance ministry sold a 1.12 billion crown tranche of one-year state bonds on August 5 at an average yield of 19.388 percent, up from 17.8 percent in the previous successful auction of similar bonds on July 22.

The National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) has been applying a tight monetary policy since summer 1996 in order to limit consumption-oriented credit expansion which last year fuelled faster-than-planned growth in the money supply.
The central bank, battling pressure on the crown, two months ago further tightened money market liquidity to limit access to crown funds.
Interbank rates have since been hovering well above 20 percent which has made budget refinancing expensive.

The 1997 budget was planned with costs for deficit refinancing at around nine percent. However, the ministry has been selling state securities at an average yield of more than 15 percent since the beginning of this year due to high interbank rates.
